title: Old Jeddah: Al-Balad
summary: How Jeddah's old town grew as a Red Sea port, why its coral-stone houses and wooden roshan windows suit the hot climate, and how it is protected today.
poll: Old buildings are worth protecting even when a city needs to grow.

versions.title: Old Jeddah
versions.text:
Jeddah is a big city by the sea. Its old part is Al-Balad. It is very old. Come and see it!

Long ago, ships came to the port. They brought goods to sell. Some men were on their way to Makkah.

A thick wall went round the town. It kept the town safe. It had gates. The wall is gone now. But some gates still stand.

The old homes are tall. They are made of coral. Coral is a stone from the sea. Wood helps hold the walls up.

The homes have big wood windows. Each one is a roshan. It has lots of small holes. The holes let the breeze in. They keep the hot sun out. Kids could look out. But no one could see in.

The streets are thin. That keeps them in the shade. It is cool there.

There is a big market, too. It is busy. You can buy spice and cloth there.

In 1925, King Abdulaziz stayed in a house here. It is Nassif House.

In 2014, the world named it a place to keep safe. Now men fix the old homes.

versions.title: Old Jeddah: Al-Balad
versions.text:
Jeddah is a large city on the coast of the Red Sea. Its oldest neighborhood is called Al-Balad, which means "the town." This historic area has been a busy place for many hundreds of years.

Long ago, Jeddah became an important port. Ships sailed in from Africa, India, and other faraway lands, and merchants traded spices, cloth, and other goods. Many travelers who came by sea were on their way to Makkah.

About five hundred years ago, a thick wall was built around the town to protect it from attacks by sea. The wall had several gates. It was taken down in the 1940s so the city could grow, but some of the old gates still stand today.

Rich merchants built tall houses, and some rose five floors or more. Builders used blocks of coral stone cut from the sea, and they added strong wooden beams to hold the walls together.

Many houses have large wooden windows called roshan. Each roshan is covered with a lattice, a pattern of thin crossing strips of wood. The lattice lets the cool sea breeze flow in while keeping out the hot sun. Families inside could look out, but people in the street could not see in.

The streets are narrow, so the tall houses on each side keep them shady.

Al-Balad also has a lively market, where people still shop for spices, cloth, and perfume.

In 1925, King Abdulaziz stayed in a famous home called Nassif House.

In 2014, Al-Balad was named a World Heritage Site. This means it is part of the heritage of the whole world. Today, workers are carefully working to restore the old houses.

versions.title: Al-Balad: The Historic Heart of Jeddah
versions.text:
Jeddah is a large city on the coast of the Red Sea, and its oldest neighborhood is called Al-Balad, which means "the town." For many centuries, this historic district has been a center of commerce, travel, and culture.

Jeddah's importance grew in the seventh century, when the caliph Uthman ibn Affan chose it as the port for Makkah. From then on, pilgrims traveling by sea arrived through Jeddah, and ships from Africa, India, and beyond brought merchants who exchanged spices, fabric, and other valuable goods.

In the early 1500s, a thick wall was constructed around the town to defend it against attacks by sea. The wall had several gates, and although it was demolished in the 1940s so that the city could expand, some of the original gates still stand today.

Wealthy merchants built tall houses, some of which rose five floors or more. Builders used blocks of coral stone cut from the Red Sea, which were relatively light, and they strengthened the walls with wooden beams.

Many houses feature large wooden windows called roshan, which are covered with an intricate lattice of thin crossing strips of wood carved by skilled artisans. The lattice provided ventilation by allowing sea breezes to circulate through the house while blocking the burning sun, and it allowed families to observe the street while remaining hidden from passersby.

Inside, many houses had a central staircase and high ceilings, and rooms on the upper floors caught the strongest breezes, which made them comfortable places to sleep during hot summer nights.

The narrow streets also helped, since the tall houses on both sides kept them shaded during the hottest hours.

Al-Balad contains lively markets, where residents and visitors still shop for spices, fabric, and perfume.

In 1925, King Abdulaziz stayed in a well-known residence called Nassif House.

In 2014, Al-Balad was named a World Heritage Site, recognizing it as part of the heritage of all humanity. Today, specialists are working to preserve and restore the old houses so that future generations can experience them.

Jeddah is a large city on the coast of the Red Sea, and its oldest neighborhood is called Al-Balad, which means "the town." For many centuries, this historic district has served as a center of commerce, travel, and culture.

Jeddah's significance grew in the seventh century, when the caliph Uthman ibn Affan selected it as the port for Makkah. From then on, pilgrims traveling by sea arrived through Jeddah, while vessels from Africa, India, and beyond brought merchants who exchanged spices, fabric, and other valuable merchandise.

In the early 1500s, a thick wall was constructed around the town to defend it against attacks by sea. The wall had several gates, and although it was demolished in the 1940s to allow the expanding city to grow, some of the original gates survive today.

Wealthy merchants commissioned tall houses, some of which rose five floors or more. Builders used blocks of coral stone quarried from the Red Sea, a material that was relatively light, and they reinforced the walls with horizontal wooden beams.

Many houses feature large wooden windows called roshan, which are covered with an intricate lattice of thin crossing strips of wood carved by skilled artisans. The lattice provided ventilation by allowing sea breezes to circulate through the house while blocking the intense sun, and it enabled families to observe the street while remaining hidden from passersby.

Inside, many houses had a central staircase and lofty ceilings, and rooms on the upper floors captured the strongest breezes, which made them comfortable places to sleep during sweltering summer nights.

The narrow streets contributed to this natural cooling, since the tall houses on both sides kept them shaded during the hottest hours of the day.

Al-Balad contains lively markets, where residents and visitors continue to shop for spices, fabric, and perfume.

Visitors who wander through the alleys today can still admire the carved doors and balconies, and in 1925, King Abdulaziz stayed in a well-known residence called Nassif House.

In 2014, Al-Balad was designated a World Heritage Site, recognizing it as part of the shared heritage of humanity. Today, specialists are working to preserve and restore the deteriorating houses so that future generations can experience them.

In the early 1500s, a substantial wall was constructed around the town to defend it against attacks by sea. The wall had several gates, and although it was demolished in the 1940s to accommodate the expanding city, some of the original gates survive today.

Wealthy merchants commissioned tall houses, some of which rose five floors or more; builders used blocks of coral stone quarried from the Red Sea, a material that was comparatively lightweight, and they reinforced the walls with horizontal wooden beams.

Many houses feature large wooden windows called roshan, which are covered with an intricate lattice of thin crossing strips of wood carved by skilled artisans. The lattice provided ventilation by allowing sea breezes to circulate through the house while blocking the intense sunlight, and it simultaneously enabled families to observe the street while remaining concealed from passersby.

Inside, many houses were organized around a central staircase and featured lofty ceilings; rooms on the upper floors captured the strongest breezes, which made them comfortable places to sleep during sweltering summer nights, long before electric air conditioning existed.

The narrow streets contributed to this natural cooling system, since the tall houses on both sides kept them shaded during the hottest hours of the day.

Al-Balad contains lively traditional markets, where residents and visitors continue to shop for spices, fabric, and perfume.

Visitors who wander through the alleys today can still admire the carved doors and balconies, and in 1925, King Abdulaziz stayed in a celebrated residence known as Nassif House.

versions.title: Al-Balad: The Historic Heart of Jeddah
versions.text:
Jeddah is a large city on the coast of the Red Sea, and its oldest neighborhood is called Al-Balad, which means "the town." For many centuries, this historic district has functioned as a center of commerce, travel, and cultural exchange between civilizations, and its legacy remains visible in nearly every alley.

Jeddah's significance increased dramatically in the seventh century, when the caliph Uthman ibn Affan selected it as the official port for Makkah. From then on, pilgrims traveling by sea arrived through Jeddah, while vessels from Africa, India, and beyond delivered merchants who exchanged spices, textiles, and other valuable merchandise.

In the early 1500s, a substantial wall was constructed around the town to defend it against maritime attacks. The fortification had several gates, and although it was demolished in the 1940s to accommodate the expanding city, some of the original gates survive today.

Wealthy merchants commissioned tall houses, some of which rose five floors or more; builders used blocks of coral stone quarried from the Red Sea, a material that was comparatively lightweight, and they reinforced the walls with horizontal wooden beams.

Many houses feature large wooden windows called roshan, which are covered with an intricate lattice of thin crossing strips of wood carved by skilled artisans. The lattice provided ventilation by permitting sea breezes to circulate throughout the house while blocking the intense sunlight, and it simultaneously enabled families to observe the street while remaining concealed from passersby.

Inside, many houses were organized around a central staircase and featured lofty ceilings; rooms on the upper floors captured the strongest breezes, which made them comfortable places to sleep during sweltering summer nights, long before electric air conditioning became widespread throughout the region.

The narrow streets contributed to this ingenious natural cooling system, since the tall houses on both sides kept them shaded during the hottest hours of the day.

Al-Balad contains lively traditional markets, where residents and visitors continue to purchase spices, textiles, and perfume.

Visitors who wander through the alleys today can still admire the carved doors and balconies, and in 1925, King Abdulaziz resided temporarily in a celebrated building known as Nassif House.

In 2014, Al-Balad was designated a World Heritage Site, recognizing it as part of the shared cultural heritage of humanity; today, specialists are working to preserve and restore the deteriorating houses so that future generations can appreciate the extraordinary craftsmanship of their ancestors.

options: It was nearby and light enough for tall houses.
It was imported by merchants on ships from India.
It never needs repairs.
It was the only stone that floats.

questions.stem: Why might the roshan be described as a clever design for Jeddah's climate?
options: It kept rain from entering the house.
It made the house look taller.
It let breezes cool the house while shading it from strong sun.
It allowed merchants to sell goods from the window.

wrong.B: Height comes from the many floors, not the roshan.
wrong.D: The article does not say goods were sold from windows.

questions.stem: How were the roshan and the narrow streets similar?
options: Both were made of coral.
Both helped keep people cool and shaded.
Both were built in the 1940s when the city grew.
Both were designed to defend the town.
